newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom stung by Sixt advert.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom stung by Sixt advert.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom AG said on Wednesday it was considering taking legal steps to counter what it called an offensive advertisement by Sixt AG.

Sixt's full-page advertisements in leading German newspapers refered to Telekom as a "state authority" just two days after the phone giant listed around a quarter of its shares in a $13 billion share offering, Europe's biggest.
Erich Sixt, founder of Germany's largest car leasing enterprise, said he considered Telekom's glitzy advertising campaign ahead of its listing a "scandal".
"It gives the impression that Telekom is a highly-developed modern technology company, but it is still bureaucratically organised and works like a state authority," he said.

Playing on Telekom's past as a part of the federal postal ministry -- the government still owns 74 percent of the company -- Sixt said in its ad: "Don't count on a state authority -- count on Germany's number one car leasing company."

Taking a stab at Telekom's 100-million-mark ($66.6 million) television advertising blitz, in which a well-known actor said Germans would be fools not to invest, Sixt's adverts said: "An actor speaks for the T-Share; the numbers speak for our stocks".
Deutsche Telekom responded sharply to the advertisements, saying they were in "clear violation of competition laws".
"We intend to counter this with all available measures. We are studying now which legal steps to take," Telekom spokesman Hans Ehnert said.
"This is a clear violation. The reference to "state authority' is misleading and wrong. It is intentionally derogatory," he added.
Erich Sixt said Telekom's advertising misled shareholders into believing the company was prepared for competition on an open German telecommunications market.

"I think the advertising campaign is a scandal," he said. "It gives the impression that Telekom is a highly-developed modern technology company, but it is still bureaucratically organised and works like a state authority."
During weeks of road shows ahead of its listing, Deutsche Telekom sought to destroy investor stereotypes of the company as an inefficient state monopoly indifferent to the needs of its customers.

Telekom chairman Ron Sommer, while admitting the company still had to work on service, has emphasised that the company has changed and that it was becoming friendlier and more sensitive to the wishes of customers.
But Sixt said Telekom's advertising gave the impression that the work had already been done.
He said there have been a number of occasions where Sixt has had to delay opening new branches because Telekom could not deliver telephone lines on time.
"I have been waiting for eight weeks for ISDN lines in Rostock, where we have 60 people waiting to go to work," he said. "The second that there is a reasonable alternative we will leave Telekom."
Sixt said the company recent signed a contract with Communications Network International (CNI), the Mannesmann telecommunications subsidiary, to set up an internal corporate network.

"We expect considerable savings from this," he said, but added that it still was not possible to connect all of Sixt's facilities with telephone lines without leasing lines from Deutsche Telekom. -- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097150 ($1=1.5011 Mark)
